spots.name: Tivoli Gardens
spots.label: Tivoli Gardens

text.geographic_location: Tivoli Gardens is in central Copenhagen, next to the Central rail station. The main entrance and the Nimb building face Vesterbrogade.
text.directions_text: Start from the Central rail station area in downtown Copenhagen, because the park sits right beside it. Head to the main entrance on Vesterbrogade, on the park's street side. This entrance is the viewpoint for the classic front shot. Rådhuspladsen, the second viewpoint, is on the city side of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: Tivoli Gardens is an amusement park and pleasure garden right in the middle of Copenhagen. It opened on 15 August 1843, which makes it the second-oldest operating amusement park in the world. From the start it mixed flower gardens, cafés and rides with buildings in the style of an imaginary Orient, and coloured lamps lit the grounds after dark. That mix is why it photographs so well. The Moorish-style Nimb building and the park gate make a bold, symmetrical front, and in the evening the lit arches and lanterns give you a ready-made subject. The wooden roller coaster Rutschebanen dates from 1914 and is still running. The Chinese-style pantomime theatre has stood here since 1874. The park is also the most visited in Scandinavia, with 4.25 million visitors in 2024, so expect people in your shots at busy times. For the classic front view, stand on the pavement on Vesterbrogade outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building. Stand square-on to the Nimb facade and fit in the gate and the lit arches. If you have time for a second angle, Rådhuspladsen gives a wider view from the city side. Tivoli Lake shows the Chinese Pagoda and Tivoli Castle reflected in the water at dusk, but that spot is inside the park, so you need an entry ticket.
text.access_note: The pavement on Vesterbrogade outside the entrance is public, but the park itself (including the lake view) needs an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go for dates and opening times.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the gate with the middle of the frame, with the facade filling the upper part. Wait for a gap in the passers-by, or let a few people stay in the lower corner to show scale. For a different view, try Rådhuspladsen for the park's skyline and lights in the distance with the square in front. Tivoli Lake, inside the park, is the choice for reflections of the Pagoda and Tivoli Castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the pavement, so the facade and gate keep a natural shape. If the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front in. Keep the phone level so the edges do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the facade is lit. If you would rather have fewer people in the frame, an early-morning visit is quieter, but the lights will not be the main feature then.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, let night mode do its work and brace your elbows against your body or a railing. Tap on the brightest lit arches to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights keep their colour and detail instead of burning out. Take a few frames and keep the sharpest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vesterbrogade (on the pavement outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building). The Moorish-style Nimb facade and the park gate, framed straight on, with the lit arches and lanterns as the focus after dark. On the pavement outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building. From here you see the Moorish-style Nimb facade and the park gate straight on, with the lit arches and lanterns as the main subject after dark.

spots.name: Nyhavn
spots.label: Nyhavn

text.geographic_location: Nyhavn is in central Copenhagen, running from the square Kongens Nytorv down to the Inner Harbour, just south of the Royal Playhouse.
text.directions_text: Start at Kongens Nytorv, the square at the inner end of Nyhavn. The Kongens Nytorv Metro station is at the far side of the square and is served by all four Copenhagen Metro lines. If you arrive by harbour bus, the stop is next to the Royal Playhouse at the mouth of Nyhavn. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: Nyhavn is the old canal harbour in the middle of Copenhagen, lined with tall, brightly painted townhouses and moored wooden ships. It was dug between 1670 and 1675 under King Christian V and was once a busy, rowdy port. Today the quay is pedestrianised and the old ships are part of a heritage harbour. It photographs well because the colours, the water and the masts all sit in one straight line, so even a quick snap looks composed. The north side has the oldest house, No. 9, dating from 1681. Hans Christian Andersen lived at several addresses here, including No. 67. The classic picture is taken from the bridge over the canal, where the full row of houses, boats and water fits in one frame. If the bridge is too crowded, Inderhavnsbroen, the footbridge and cycle bridge across the harbour mouth, gives a view of Nyhavn from the water side. Expect people on the quayside and café terraces, so leave a little space around your subject and take a few shots as the crowd shifts. Keep the phone steady against the railing, and wipe the lens first, as harbour air can leave a faint film on it.
text.access_note: The quay is an open, pedestrianised public space and the museum ships can be seen from the cobbles; check the official site before you go if you want to board a ship or visit a museum.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the quay up with one of the lower grid lines so the houses stay upright. Put the boats in the lower third and the houses in the middle, with a little sky above. For a different view, walk to Inderhavnsbroen for Nyhavn seen across the water; it opens for boats, so stand clear of the central section when the horn sounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking houses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge is busy and you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a single boat, a mast or a row of window frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide recommends late afternoon. The north-side houses are said to catch good light mainly in the morning and early afternoon in summer, and the terraces fill up from late morning, so going early means fewer people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the bright colours do not wash out. Take a Live Photo too, as boats and passers-by can give you a better frame than the still you aimed for.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nyhavnsbroen (bridge at the canal's inner end; sources disagree on which end, so check on the map). The full row of coloured canal houses with moored wooden boats and the water in one frame. The aim is a photo that shows the full row of coloured canal houses, the moored wooden boats and the water in one frame.

spots.name: Rosenborg Castle
spots.label: Rosenborg Castle

text.geographic_location: Rosenborg Castle stands inside Kongens Have (the King's Garden) in Copenhagen. Next to it are the barracks of the Royal Life Guards.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. From there the castle lies about 85 metres to the south-east, roughly 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Rosenborg Castle is a Dutch Renaissance building in Copenhagen, set in the King's Garden (Kongens Have). It began as a country summerhouse in 1606, was extended several times and reached its present form by 1624. Christian IV was behind it, and it is one of his many building projects. Danish rulers lived here until around 1710, and it was used as a royal residence only twice after that, both times in emergencies. Today it is a museum of the Royal Collections and holds the Crown Jewels. It has been open to the public since 1838.

It photographs well because the castle stands in open parkland. In summer, flowers bloom in the castle garden, which can add colour in the foreground. The garden is the country's oldest royal garden and is busy with visitors, so wait a moment for a clear gap in the people on the paths.

Start with a wide shot of the full castle, then move in with zoom for the towers, rooflines and brickwork. Keep your phone level so the tall walls do not lean. Interior photography, if allowed at all, is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
text.access_note: The castle is open to the public for tours as a museum and the garden is a public park, but access and tickets can change, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the castle on one of the vertical lines, with the building in the upper two-thirds and paths or flowerbeds below. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls stay straight. Wait for a gap in the walkers if you want an empty foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole castle and its garden. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, roof details and windows. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk much closer and want the full height in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In summer the flowers in the garden add colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brick and roof detail do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. This gives you the castle with open garden in front of it.
